newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU governments urged to reform social schemes.
newsitem.headline: EU governments urged to reform social schemes.

text.p: European Union governments must reform their social protection systems to take account of new working styles, the aging population and the changing role of men and women, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
They should, for example, consider providing "employability insurance" to finance training for workers who lose their jobs instead of traditional unemployment compensation, it said in a report.

"Today, with the labour market rapidly evolving to respond to changing needs and demands and becoming increasingly skills-based, it has become essential that those seeking employment are prepared to acquire new and different skills," it said.
Governments should also cooperate to reverse the trend of rising taxes on labour to make it more attractive for employers to create jobs, especially for low-skilled workers, the Commission said.
Repeating one of its longstanding ideas, the Commission said high labour taxes could be replaced by environmental or energy taxes.

Noting that the aging population was putting strains on government pension schemes, the EU executive said it would issue a discussion paper this year on ways to ensure that governments provide a secure environment for company pensions.
The Commission said it would also assess this year possible reforms to public pension plans, for example by finding ways to keep people in work rather than taking early retirement.
It said it would also present initiatives on ways to set higher standards for the care of children and other dependents as part of an effort to help workers reconcile their family and working lives.

EU governments must also find a way to "individualise" social security benefits, that is separate them from the worker's marital status, without jeopardising the economic position of women, the Commission said.

"Derived rights" -- those earned by wives of employed men, for example -- put the beneficiary in a dependent position, it noted. They leave women vulnerable in cases of divorce and can discourage them from entering the labour market, it said.
